conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new moms. Over the next few minutes I’d like to walk through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) with you. It’s a short, 10-question tool that helps us see how you’ve been coping emotionally during the past week of new motherhood. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety issue, so please answer as honestly as you feel comfortable. I’ll ask each question conversationally, we’ll jot your answers, and then we’ll review what the results might mean and talk about next steps. Ready to start?

First, how have you been able to enjoy things lately—little moments of laughter, music, a favorite show? What’s that felt like for you over the past seven days?

Honestly, not much feels fun anymore. I’ll put on the show I used to love while I nurse, and it’s just… flat. I’ll catch myself half-smiling maybe once or twice, but the second the episode ends I’m right back to this dull, heavy feeling. Music I used to dance around to just sounds like noise now. Even when my sister sent me that funny video, I laughed for a second and then felt empty again.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I’ll catch myself laughing at something small—like when the baby makes that silly milk-drunk face—but it feels kind of forced, and the laugh dies off fast. Most of the time I can’t really find the funny side, even when everyone else is chuckling.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now when I think about doing anything I just feel… flat, like, “what’s the point?” I still go, because I know I should, but there’s no spark of looking forward to it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If he spits up more than usual, my brain jumps straight to “I must’ve eaten something wrong,” or if he’s fussy I’m convinced it’s because I’m not soothing him right. My partner says I’m too hard on myself, but I keep replaying every little thing and thinking I’m messing this mom thing up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting on the couch, baby’s asleep in the bassinet, and suddenly my chest feels tight and I’m sure something awful is about to happen—like he’ll stop breathing or I’ll drop him when I stand up. There’s no real trigger; the fear just barges in and I can’t shake it for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… it’s happened a few times. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t catch my breath—like I need to run out of the room even though nothing’s happening. Once I was just folding his onesies and suddenly felt sure something terrible was about to happen. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s like the second I open my eyes the list of “shoulds” crashes down—laundry, bottles, texts I haven’t answered—and I feel this weight on my chest. I still push through and get stuff done, but it’s like wading through thick mud; everything feels harder than it should.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

A few nights this week I’ve lain there after the 2 a.m. feed, exhausted but my brain won’t shut off. I keep replaying every little thing I might’ve done wrong, worrying something will happen to the baby, and then I’m wide-awake for an hour or more. It’s not every single night, but it’s happened several times.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… that’s been most days lately. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. I’ll cry when I’m alone—sometimes in the shower, sometimes while I’m rocking him—and I can’t always explain why. It’s not every single minute, but it’s definitely there more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

A couple of times this week it’s hit me that hard. Yesterday I was trying to get him down for a nap and he just wouldn’t settle, and suddenly I was sobbing at the side of the crib—had to put him down in the bassinet and go splash water on my face so he wouldn’t see me like that. It’s not constant tears, but when it comes it feels like a wave I can’t stop.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…yes. A couple of times, just brief flashes—like I’ll be standing at the kitchen counter and picture myself running the knife the wrong way, or imagine not waking up if I took too many of those pills. They’re gone as fast as they come, I haven’t made any plans or anything, but they’ve definitely popped into my head this week.

You've shared that the joy you used to feel has faded since your baby arrived; most days carry a heavy, gray mood, laughter feels forced, and even simple outings seem pointless. You described frequent, unexplained <sym>anxiety</sym> and sudden <sym>panic</sym> with racing heart, persistent <sym>self-blame</sym> about mothering, and several tearful episodes that leave you feeling overwhelmed. Most concerning, brief <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym> have surfaced this week. You are working incredibly hard to care for your little one while carrying these painful feelings, and that emotional load deserves immediate support and attention.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>She reports only occasional, fleeting laughter that feels forced and says she usually cannot find the funny side, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient reports a near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, aligning with "Hardly at all".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, pervasive self-blame across multiple scenarios, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily intrusive, unprovoked anxiety episodes with physical symptoms and catastrophic fears, aligning with "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden racing heart, breathlessness, urge to flee, and anticipatory dread occurring multiple times without trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed most days and tasks feel disproportionately hard, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports several nights of significant sleep disruption linked to unhappiness, worry, and rumination, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness, frequent unexplained crying, and a persistent "gray cloud" mood, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Response clearly indicates crying episodes happening several times in the past week, aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges recurrent intrusive self-harm thoughts several times this week, fitting "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score ≥14 plus Item 10 ≥1 signals urgent concern under EPDS guidelines. You endorsed pervasive <sym>low mood</sym>, near-complete loss of interest, daily <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, multiple <sym>panic</sym> episodes, and recurring <sym>self-harm images</sym>, meeting core <med>DSM-5 criteria</med> for Major <med>Depressive</med> Disorder with peripartum onset. <quote>I picture myself running the knife the wrong way</quote> indicates active, though fleeting, suicidal ideation requiring immediate safety planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Mobilise partner or trusted adult to stay with you and baby until medical review; keep kitchen and bathroom items secured
3. Call 988 (US) or your local crisis line if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
4. Begin gentle <sym>sleep-hygiene</sym>: 30-min wind-down, dim lights, hand baby to support person for one night-time feed if possible
5. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks or sooner if symptoms change; maintain regular contact with provider
6. Consider referral to <med>CBT</med>-based support group or <med>IPT</med> therapist specialising in postpartum mood
7. Encourage daily 10-min outdoor walk and hydration; reduce self-criticism by noting one thing done well each day
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note (Patient: self-report)

**Primary symptoms endorsed**  
- Persistent low mood, frequent crying spells  
- Marked anhedonia (“flat,” no “spark”)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt about mothering  
- Daily free-floating anxiety, episodic panic (racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to rumination  
- Feeling overwhelmed / inability to cope most days  

**Observed patterns**  
- Symptoms present “most days,” beginning post-delivery  
- Functional impact: difficulty completing tasks, social withdrawal despite attempts to engage  
- Safety: fleeting self-harm images (no plan or intent reported)  

**Screening significance**  
- Meets threshold items for possible Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety  
- Safety flag: presence of self-harm ideation warrants immediate risk assessment  

**Plan**  
- Recommend same-day clinician review for comprehensive evaluation, safety planning, and discussion of supports.
